bai.ten: The Milky Way: our city of stars
bai.moTa: Hundreds of billions of stars, a central black hole, and two giant bubbles
bai.yChinh: The Sun is one of the Milky Way’s hundreds of billions of stars, 26,700 light-years from its center. Stars far from the center orbit almost as fast as stars closer in, a sign of **dark matter**. At the very center lies Sagittarius A*, a black hole of 4.3 million solar masses. Two giant bubbles rise above and below it.
bai.giaiThich:
Each point of light here represents millions of stars. The reconstruction reflects our current understanding: a **central bar of stars**, **four main spiral arms**, and a thin disk only about 1,000 light-years thick compared with its 100,000-light-year width. We are inside the Galaxy, so parts of this map are uncertain, especially the far side of the center.

The spiral arms are **density waves**, rather than fixed strings of stars. The nearly flat rotation curve provides evidence for dark matter. The Fermi bubbles (2010, gamma rays) and eROSITA bubbles (2020, X-rays) are probably traces of energetic outbursts in the central region.
bai.conSo.1: **100–400 billion** stars. The stellar disk is about 100,000 light-years across and about 1,000 light-years thick.
bai.conSo.2: **26,700 light-years** (8.2 kpc): our distance from the galactic center.
bai.conSo.3: **About 10¹¹ solar masses**: the mass inside the Sun’s orbit, calculated from $v^2R/G$.
bai.conSo.4: **Sagittarius A*** is a black hole of 4.3 million solar masses. Its event horizon radius is 12.7 million km. The star S2 orbits it every 16 years.
bai.conSo.5: **25,000 light-years**: the height of each Fermi bubble. The eROSITA bubbles reach 45,000 light-years.
bai.conSo.6: **2.5 million light-years**: the distance to the Andromeda Galaxy, which approaches at about 110 km/s.
bai.hieuDung: **No one has photographed the Milky Way from outside.** Every panoramic view, including this model, is reconstructed from observations of stellar distances and velocities, hydrogen gas, and radio waves. Voyager 1 has traveled only one light-day. To photograph the Galaxy from outside would require traveling tens of thousands of light-years.
bai.nguon: GRAVITY Collaboration 2018–2022 (distance R₀, mass of Sgr A*, orbit of S2); Event Horizon Telescope 2022; Reid et al. 2019 (spiral arms, rotation speed); Bland-Hawthorn and Gerhard 2016, ARA&A 54, 529 (structure, bar, stellar and gas masses, total Milky Way mass); Su, Slatyer and Finkbeiner 2010 (Fermi bubbles); Predehl et al. 2020 (eROSITA bubbles); van der Marel et al. 2012, ApJ 753, 8 (Andromeda’s velocity and orbit); Sawala et al. 2025, Nature Astronomy (probability of a Milky Way–Andromeda merger). Constants: CODATA 2018, IAU 2012.
bai.baiGiang.mucTieu.1: Describe the Milky Way’s shape: its disk, central bulge, bar, spiral arms, and halo.
bai.baiGiang.mucTieu.2: Explain how a spiral arm can be a density wave while its individual stars keep changing.
bai.baiGiang.mucTieu.3: Calculate the mass inside the Sun’s orbit from $v^2R/G$ and interpret a rotation curve as evidence for dark matter.
bai.baiGiang.mucTieu.4: Use Kepler’s law to infer the mass of the black hole Sagittarius A* from the orbit of the star S2.
bai.baiGiang.mucTieu.5: Locate the Milky Way among its neighboring galaxies.
bai.baiGiang.buoc.1.ten: A disk with a bar at its center
bai.baiGiang.buoc.1.noiDung:
You are looking at the Milky Way from outside, at an angle above the disk. Each bright dot represents millions of stars. The Galaxy as a whole contains about 100–400 billion stars. It has three main parts:

- The **disk** is about 100,000 light-years across but only about 1,000 light-years thick, as thin in proportion as a CD. The Sun lies in the disk.
- The **central bulge and bar** form the yellow-orange region of older stars in the middle, elongated into a **bar** about 30,000 light-years long. The Milky Way is a {{thiên hà xoắn ốc có thanh|barred spiral galaxy}}.
- The **spiral arms** are the brighter, bluer bands winding around the disk, rich in young stars and gas.

A sparse, nearly spherical **halo** surrounds them all. It contains globular clusters, shown as scattered yellow dots.

> [Hiểu sai thường gặp] No one has photographed the Milky Way from outside. This view was reconstructed from measured distances and velocities of stars, hydrogen gas, and molecular clouds. Dust obscures the far side of the center, so the reconstruction there is less certain.

> [Thử ngay] Hover over the central bulge, the arms, the Sun, or a globular cluster for names and data. Look edge-on to see the dark dust lane crossing the bulge.
> [[View from above|tren]] [[View the disk edge-on|ngang]] [[Overview|toan]]
bai.baiGiang.buoc.2.ten: Spiral arms as waves: stars pass through them
bai.baiGiang.buoc.2.noiDung:
Speed up time and look down from above. A star near the center completes an orbit sooner than a more distant star. In this model, a star 13,000 light-years from the center takes about 107 million years per orbit, while the Sun takes about 219 million.

If an arm were a fixed string of stars, the difference would wind it up: every billion years, the inner part would complete nearly **5 extra turns** relative to the outer part. The Milky Way is more than 10 billion years old and its arms are still open. A widely accepted explanation is that an arm is a {{sóng mật độ|density wave}}.

Think of a traffic jam on a highway. Cars enter it, slow down, and leave; the jam persists as the cars in it change. Stars and gas likewise pass through an arm. Gas is compressed there and new stars form. The brightest blue stars live only a few million years, so they die before they can leave the arm. This makes the arms bright and blue.

> [Lưu ý] In the model the arm pattern rotates uniformly at 25 km/s per kiloparsec, completing one turn in about 246 million years. Disk stars brighten as they cross an arm, while the particles representing young stars follow the arms. This illustrates the density-wave idea; it is not a dynamical simulation.

> [Thử ngay] Drag the test star (the green star with rays) toward or away from the center. Near the center it overtakes the arms; farther out the arms overtake it. An illustrative chime sounds every time it crosses an arm.
> [[Run at 20 million years per second|nhanh]] [[Pause|dung]] [[View from above|tren]]
bai.baiGiang.buoc.2.thuThach.de: Find the **corotation circle**, where the test star takes exactly as long to orbit as the spiral pattern does (246 million years). There the star stands still relative to the arms and you hear no chime. Complete the challenge by bringing the two periods within 3% of each other.
bai.baiGiang.buoc.2.thuThach.goiY: Close to the center the test star rotates faster than the spiral pattern. Drag it outward until it stays still relative to an arm. The data panel shows both periods. In the model the circle lies about 30,000 light-years from the center.
bai.baiGiang.buoc.3.noiDung:
The Sun (the yellow dot with an arrow) lies about **26,700 light-years**, or 8.2 kiloparsecs, from the center, more than halfway to the edge of the disk. It lies in the **Orion Arm**, a short spur between the two major arms Sagittarius (inward) and Perseus (outward).

The yellow trail shows the Sun’s path over the last 200 million years. As we calculated in Lesson 1, one orbit takes about 220 million years, a {{năm thiên hà|galactic year}}.

The Sun also moves up and down through the plane of the disk, like a horse on a carousel. It is currently a few tens of light-years north of the plane.

> [Lưu ý] The model’s vertical oscillation (amplitude 300 light-years, period 85 million years) is illustrative. Observational estimates vary between authors. The Sun is also drawn billions of times larger than its actual size.

> [Con số] The distance of 8.2 kpc was measured by tracking stars orbiting the central black hole (GRAVITY 2019–2021). Knowing the orbit’s size in AU and its angular size on the sky lets us calculate the distance.

> [Thử ngay] [[Fly to the Sun|mt]] [[View from above|tren]] [[Return to the present|nay]]
bai.baiGiang.buoc.4.ten: A flat rotation curve and dark matter
bai.baiGiang.buoc.4.noiDung:
The green points are three stars at 26,700, 38,000, and 50,000 light-years from the center. Measurements show **nearly the same speed** for all three, about 230 km/s. The graph of speed against distance in the controls is almost horizontal: a flat {{đường cong quay|rotation curve}}.

If nearly all the mass lay inside the Sun’s orbit, just as the Sun holds most of the mass of the Solar System, stars farther out would have to move more slowly according to Kepler’s law:

$$ v = \sqrt{\frac{GM}{r}} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad v \propto \frac{1}{\sqrt{r}} $$

The pink points show those three stars moving at Keplerian speeds. At 50,000 light-years the speed would be just 168 km/s, and the star would fall behind. Real stars do not slow down that much. The outer regions must contain additional mass we cannot see: {{vật chất tối|dark matter}}.

+++ Go deeper: weighing the Galaxy with the Sun’s speed
Gravity supplies the centripetal force: $GM/R^2 = v^2/R$. The mass enclosed by the orbit is therefore

$$ M = \frac{v^2 R}{G} = \frac{(2{,}3 \times 10^{5})^2 \times 2{,}53 \times 10^{20}}{6{,}67 \times 10^{-11}} \approx 2{,}0 \times 10^{41}\ \text{kg} \approx 1{,}0 \times 10^{11}\ M_\odot $$

This formula is exact for a spherical mass distribution; for a flat disk the estimate is off by a few tens of percent. If $v$ is constant, $M = v^2R/G$ grows in proportion to $R$. Double the radius and you double the enclosed mass, although little light comes from those outer regions. The Milky Way’s stars and gas together amount to only about $6 \times 10^{10}\ M_\odot$, while the total mass including the outskirts is about $10^{12}\ M_\odot$. Most of it is dark matter.
+++

> [Thử ngay] Drag the test star (the green star with rays) outward. The pink star shows how it would move at the Keplerian speed. Two sustained tones have pitches proportional to the two speeds (2 Hz per km/s, a conversion into the audible range). The tone for the real star stays nearly constant, while the Keplerian tone drops as you move outward.
> [[Speed up|nhanh]] [[Reset|lai]] [[View from above|quay]]
bai.baiGiang.buoc.4.thuThach.de: Place the test star where the Keplerian speed is just **3/4** of the measured speed. There the mass inside the star’s orbit must be $(4/3)^2 \approx 1{,}78$ times the mass inside the Sun’s orbit. Complete the challenge by getting the ratio within 0.015 of its target.
bai.baiGiang.buoc.4.thuThach.goiY: $\sqrt{R_0/R} = 3/4$, so $R = 16R_0/9 \approx 47\,500$ light-years. The two tones are then a perfect fourth apart (a frequency ratio of 3 : 4).
bai.baiGiang.buoc.5.ten: Sagittarius A*: the central black hole
bai.baiGiang.buoc.5.noiDung:
At the very center lies the {{lỗ đen siêu nặng|supermassive black hole}} Sagittarius A*, with about **4.3 million solar masses**. Its symbol is enlarged hundreds of millions of times. The actual event horizon radius is only 12.7 million km, roughly 1/5 of Mercury’s distance from the Sun.

Astronomers weigh it using Kepler’s law from Lesson 1. The star **S2** orbits Sgr A* every **16 years** on a highly elongated ellipse. At closest approach it comes within 120 AU and travels at about 7,650 km/s. For a central mass $M$ measured in solar masses:

$$ T^2 = \frac{a^3}{M} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad a = (M T^2)^{1/3} = (4{,}3 \times 10^{6} \times 16^2)^{1/3} \approx 1\,030\ \text{AU} $$

The observed orbit size agrees with this value. Only a black hole could fit that much mass into so little space.

> [Lịch sử] In 2018 the GRAVITY team measured the gravitational redshift of S2’s light at closest approach, as predicted by general relativity. In 2020 they measured the precession of S2’s orbit (Lesson 13). In 2022 the Event Horizon Telescope released an image of Sgr A*’s shadow (Lesson 15).

> [Thử ngay] A test star at the center follows an elongated ellipse like S2. Drag the blue dot, the farthest point of the orbit, inward or outward. A larger orbit has a longer period according to $T = \sqrt{a^3/M}$. The orbit is enlarged about 130,000 times, and the black hole is magnified even more. The separate clock here runs at 2 years per second. A bell rings each time the star sweeps past the point nearest the black hole.
> [[Fly to the center|tam]] [[Overview|toan]]
bai.baiGiang.buoc.5.thuThach.de: Drag the test star’s orbit until one revolution takes exactly **16 years**, like S2. Aim for a period within half a year of the target.
bai.baiGiang.buoc.5.thuThach.goiY: The calculation above gives $a \approx 1\,030$ AU. The label next to the test star shows $a$ and $T$.
bai.baiGiang.buoc.6.noiDung:
Look at the disk edge-on. Two pairs of bubbles rise above and below the galactic center.

- The **Fermi bubbles** (pink), discovered in 2010 in gamma-ray images from the Fermi telescope, extend about **25,000 light-years** on each side.
- The **eROSITA bubbles** (orange and larger), discovered in 2020 in X-ray images, extend about **45,000 light-years** on each side.

The naked eye cannot see them. They contain very hot gas and high-energy particles, probably produced by outbursts in the central region a few million to a few tens of millions of years ago. The black hole may have rapidly accreted gas, or intense star formation may have supplied the energy. The cause remains under debate.

> [Lưu ý] The bubbles are drawn smooth and symmetric for clarity. The actual bubbles have uneven edges and are asymmetric.

> [Thử ngay] [[Edge-on view|bong]] [[Hide the bubbles|tat]] [[Show them again|bat]]
bai.baiGiang.buoc.7.ten: Our neighbors: the Magellanic Clouds and Andromeda
bai.baiGiang.buoc.7.noiDung:
Zoom far out. The Milky Way has two small companion galaxies visible to the naked eye in the southern sky: the **Large Magellanic Cloud** (160,000 light-years) and the **Small Magellanic Cloud** (200,000 light-years).

Much farther away is the **Andromeda Galaxy (M31)**, about the size of the Milky Way and **2.5 million light-years** away. The light we see left it before humans appeared. Andromeda is **approaching** the Milky Way’s center at about 110 km/s.

A rough estimate: 2.5 million light-years divided by 110 km/s gives about 6.8 billion years. But the two galaxies attract each other and speed up as they approach. Astronomers used to think a collision in about 4–5 billion years was certain. A 2025 calculation based on Hubble and Gaia measurements shows that it is **not certain**: Andromeda’s sideways velocity is still poorly known, and the pull of M33 and the Large Magellanic Cloud shifts the orbit. The chance that the two galaxies merge within the next 10 billion years is only about **one half**; the chance of a head-on collision within the next 4–5 billion years is only about 2%. If they do collide, individual stars would almost never hit each other, because the spaces between them are so large.

The Milky Way, Andromeda, Triangulum (M33), and several dozen smaller galaxies make up the {{Nhóm Địa phương|Local Group}}.

> [Lưu ý] As measured from the Sun, Andromeda approaches at about 300 km/s. Much of that comes from the Sun itself: its speed is 230 km/s (Lesson 1) and its motion is about 37° from the direction to Andromeda, contributing about 185 km/s. Subtracting that contribution gives about 110 km/s.

> [Thử ngay] [[See our neighbors|xom]] [[Return to the Milky Way|toan]]

bai.baiGiang.congThuc.2.y: This applies when nearly all the mass is inside the orbit. The Milky Way’s departure from this law is evidence for dark matter.
bai.baiGiang.congThuc.3.ten: Kepler’s law for any central mass
bai.baiGiang.congThuc.3.y: For S2, $T = 16$ years and $a \approx 1\,030$ AU give $M \approx 4{,}3$ million.
bai.baiGiang.congThuc.4.y: For Sgr A*: about 12.7 million km.
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.1.hoi: Why have the Milky Way’s spiral arms not wound up tightly over billions of years?
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.1.chon.1: All stars rotate at the same angular speed, like a rigid body
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.1.chon.2: The arms are density waves: stars pass through while the pattern persists
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.1.chon.3: The central black hole holds the arms fixed
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.1.chon.4: The Milky Way formed only recently
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.1.giai: Stars near the center complete an orbit much sooner than distant stars, so a fixed string of stars would wind up. An arm is a region of crowding, like a traffic jam: stars enter it and leave again. The central black hole is too light compared with the whole Galaxy (only about one two-hundred-thousandth of its mass) to shape the arms.
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.2.hoi: A star twice as far from the galactic center as the Sun orbits at exactly the Sun’s speed. How does the mass inside its orbit compare with the mass inside the Sun’s orbit?
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.2.giai: $M = v^2R/G$. At the same $v$, doubling $R$ doubles $M$. If the enclosed mass stayed the same, with no added mass in the outer region, the star would move more slowly, at just $230/\sqrt 2 \approx 163$ km/s.
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.3.hoi: What does the Milky Way’s flat rotation curve tell us?
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.3.chon.2: There is a great deal of unseen mass far from the center
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.3.chon.3: There is no black hole at the galactic center
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.3.chon.4: The law of gravity is wrong at every distance
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.3.giai: Distant stars still orbit rapidly, so the mass inside their orbits keeps growing with radius, even where stars and gas become sparse. Dark matter is the widely accepted explanation. Some theories modify gravity at very low accelerations, which is quite different from saying that it is wrong at every distance.
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.4.hoi: S2 orbits Sgr A* every 16 years. If the black hole had 8 times its mass and the period were still 16 years, how would the orbit’s semi-major axis change?
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.4.giai: $a = (MT^2)^{1/3}$. Increasing $M$ by a factor of 8 increases $a$ by a factor of $8^{1/3} = 2$.
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.5.hoi: From the Sun, Andromeda approaches at about 300 km/s. Why do books say it approaches the Milky Way at about 110 km/s?
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.5.chon.2: Because much of the 300 km/s comes from the Sun itself moving toward Andromeda as it orbits the galactic center
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.5.giai: This is the reference-frame lesson from Lesson 1 again: speed depends on the frame in which it is measured. Subtract the Sun’s 230 km/s orbital motion around the galactic center to find Andromeda’s velocity relative to the Milky Way.
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.6.hoi: Why are astronomers confident there is a black hole at the galactic center, even though an ordinary telescope cannot see it directly?
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.6.dap: The orbits of stars near the center, especially S2 (16 years per orbit and only 120 AU away at closest approach), let us use Kepler’s law to measure the central mass: about 4.3 million solar masses. All that mass fits inside a region smaller than S2’s closest orbital distance. No star cluster or other object besides a black hole can be so massive and compact. GRAVITY later measured S2’s gravitational redshift (2018), and the EHT imaged Sgr A*’s shadow (2022).
bai.baiGiang.docThem.1: GRAVITY Collaboration 2018, A&A 615, L15: measurement of S2’s gravitational redshift as it passed close to Sgr A*.
bai.baiGiang.docThem.2: Event Horizon Telescope 2022, ApJL 930, L12: an image of the shadow of Sagittarius A*.
bai.baiGiang.docThem.3: B. Ryden, *Introduction to Cosmology* (2nd edition, 2016): the section on dark matter, including galaxy rotation curves.
bai.baiGiang.docThem.4: K. S. Thorne, *Black Holes and Time Warps* (1994): supermassive black holes in the centers of galaxies.
bai.baiGiang.thuatNgu.1.nghia: A disk-shaped galaxy with spiral arms and a central region elongated into a bar of stars. The Milky Way is one example.
bai.baiGiang.thuatNgu.2.nghia: A region where stars and gas are crowded together. Its pattern rotates uniformly at its own angular speed, different from that of the stars; stars and gas pass through it. This is the main explanation for spiral arms.
bai.baiGiang.thuatNgu.3.nghia: A graph of the orbital speed of stars and gas against their distance from a galaxy’s center.
bai.baiGiang.thuatNgu.4.nghia: Matter that neither emits nor absorbs light and reveals itself through gravity. It accounts for most of the Milky Way’s mass.
bai.baiGiang.thuatNgu.5.nghia: A black hole with millions to billions of solar masses, found at the center of most large galaxies.
bai.baiGiang.thuatNgu.6.nghia: A group of several dozen galaxies about 10 million light-years across, including the Milky Way, Andromeda, Triangulum, and their smaller companions.
